items.title: Scoped DbContext, and the captive-dependency trap
items.body:
AppDbContext is scoped: one instance per HTTP request. Every repository injected in that request shares the same change tracker, so one SaveChangesAsync flushes all their changes in one transaction, and the context is disposed when the request ends. Inject it into a singleton and it becomes a captive dependency: it lives forever, accumulates tracked entities, and eventually throws or returns stale data.

- Separate contexts per repository is not the failure described; the problem is one context living too long.
- A captured context is never disposed, rather than disposed too early.
- Connection pooling is not mentioned.

excerpts.quote: the context lives forever, accumulates entities, and eventually throws or returns stale data.

items.title: The handler guard is the only tenant check here
items.body:
The key is right. `RepositoryBase.GetByIdAsync` is `await Set.FindAsync([id], ct)`: a primary-key load with no tenant or owner condition. EF query filters could add one, but the codebase has a single `HasQueryFilter`, on users (`u => u.IsActive`).

- No filter exists on EventType.
- `RepositoryBase` adds no Where clause.
- `AppDbContext` receives `ICurrentTenantService` in its constructor but never uses it to filter rows.

excerpts.quote: await Set.FindAsync([id], ct);
The source-level guard is therefore the only tenant/owner check on this path, not a second layer.

items.title: Core idea: know what a small fix does not prove
items.body:
The course is careful to separate one proven rule from everything else. The guard it adds is about scope: a wrong host or tenant in the request. A good reviewer then asks what such a guard does not cover, and keeps a written list of known gaps instead of assuming the change fixed more than it did.

The review chapter lists four verified findings the lab left open. Before reading each one, look at the code it names and form your own view on four questions: how the tenant is found for a caller who sends no token, how an error code is turned into an HTTP status, which filters the conflict query uses, and what (if anything) stops two invitees from booking the same slot at the same moment. Then compare your answers with the findings and the tests each one proposes.

excerpts.quote: ## Verified review findings the lab did not fix (checked 2026-10-06)
each names the test that would prove it.

readMore.why: Findings A to D, each with file and line evidence.
How the runtime harness counts repository calls.

items.title: Nothing throttles the anonymous endpoints
items.body:
Program.cs registers authentication, authorization, controllers, Swagger and CORS, and its request pipeline runs exception handling, logging, CORS, tenant resolution, authentication and authorization before the controllers. No rate limiter is registered anywhere, and BookingsController.Create is [AllowAnonymous], so a script can send as many requests as it likes and every one reaches the action. The critique files this as RISK-006 and suggests AddRateLimiter with a sliding window on the public endpoints.

- CORS is a browser rule: a script simply ignores it.
- The JWT handler authenticates; it keeps no quota.
- ASP.NET Core applies no rate limit unless you add one.

A related upstream finding on the other public endpoint: in the pinned code, available-slots answers 500 as soon as its handler reaches the schedule lookup. ScheduleRepository uses Include("_rules"), but the owned collection is mapped as the Rules navigation, and EF Core refuses an include path that names no navigation when it compiles the query (an EF Core 10.0.12 probe throws InvalidOperationException for this shape; owned rules load without any Include).

excerpts.quote: Public endpoint — invitees book without authentication.
builder.OwnsMany(s => s.Rules, rules =>

items.title: Three validation layers that overlap on purpose
items.body:
Booking input meets three layers. CreateBookingValidator checks format: a valid email, a future start time, a non-empty name. Booking.Create() checks business rules such as start before end and not in the past. The database enforces the unique cancellation token and foreign keys. Some checks repeat, and the guide says that is intentional: the domain doesn't trust that the validator ran, and the validator doesn't trust that domain rules match.

- Nothing marks the overlap as accidental or due for removal.
- The database does enforce the unique cancellation token.
- FluentValidation is not meant to own business rules; slot availability is outside its job.

excerpts.quote: The layers are intentionally overlapping — the domain doesn't trust that the validator ran.

items.title: Update(aggregate) writes every column
items.body:
When EF tracks an entity it loaded and you change one property, the save writes only the changed columns. But NetCalendy's `repository.Update(aggregate)` calls `db.Set<T>().Update(aggregate)`, which marks the entire entity as modified. The resulting UPDATE writes every column even if only one changed. The guide calls this a full-update pattern and suggests explicit property tracking for high write volume.

- Only-changed-columns is the tracked-entity behavior that Update() overrides.
- No version-only update is involved.
- Update() attaches the entity and marks it modified, so the save does write.

excerpts.quote: every column is written even if only one changed.

items.title: The order of two checks decides what leaks
items.body:
The key is right. Line 27 checks existence, tenant and owner; line 29 checks `IsActive`. For an event that is both inactive and someone else's, line 27 already returns NotFound, so the caller never learns that the event exists or that it is inactive.

- Inactive would only be returned for an in-scope event.
- The conflict query (line 33) is after both checks, so it is never reached.
- A `Result` carries one error; the handler returns at the first failure.

excerpts.quote: scope is tested on line 27 and state on line 29
if (!eventType.IsActive)

items.title: The tenant comes from the JWT claim only
items.body:
The key is right. `CurrentTenantService.TenantId` reads `HttpContext.User.FindFirst("tenant_id")` and parses it as a Guid. The handler calls `TenantId.From(currentTenant.TenantId!.Value)`.

- `TenantResolutionMiddleware` writes `context.Items["TenantId"]`, but nothing in `src/` reads it.
- The command has no tenant field; the map says tenant identity is not copied from the command.
- The handler never reads request headers; the X-Tenant-Slug header is used only by the middleware.

excerpts.quote: FindFirst("tenant_id")
nothing in `src/` reads `Items["TenantId"]`

items.title: What a real Postgres container catches
items.body:
NetCalendy's integration tests start a real Postgres container through Testcontainers and do not mock the database layer. The critique lists what that catches and mock-based tests miss entirely: EF Core query issues, missing indexes, migration errors, and SQL-level constraint violations.

- Validator rules, handler branches, Result mapping and DTO shapes are what a mock-based test already exercises; a real database adds nothing there.
- Races and isolation problems are a separate risk (RISK-003), and the parallel test for it is still a ticket to write.

A useful habit: when you add a query, ask which of the four it could hit, and make sure an integration test runs it.

excerpts.quote: This catches EF Core query issues, missing indexes, migration errors, and SQL-level constraint violations that mock-based tests miss entirely.

items.title: What the dependency rule buys in practice
items.body:
The critique confirms the inward dependency rule: Domain has no EF Core, HTTP or MediatR handler imports, Application has no HttpContext, and every boundary crossing goes through an interface. Its consequence is concrete: you can replace PostgreSQL with SQLite for tests, replace the MediatR pipeline with a raw handler call, or swap controllers for gRPC, all without touching domain or application logic.

- Separate deployment of the layers is not claimed.
- The critique still values real-database integration tests; the rule does not replace them.
- Domain must not depend on EF Core, so sharing a DbContext with it would break the rule.

excerpts.quote: you can replace PostgreSQL with SQLite for tests, replace the MediatR pipeline with a raw handler call, or swap controllers for gRPC

items.title: The event type decides how long a booking is
items.body:
The key is right. Line 31 is `var endTime = cmd.StartTime.AddMinutes(eventType.Duration.Minutes);`. The caller chooses only the start; the length comes from the stored event type.

- The command has no end-time field.
- Schedules decide which slots are offered, not the length of a booking.
- The invitee timezone is validated in `Invitee.Create`; it does not set the booking length.

excerpts.quote: cmd.StartTime.AddMinutes(eventType.Duration.Minutes)
Duration comes from the selected event; the client cannot independently choose an end time in this command.

items.title: Removing a column takes two deploys
items.body:
No migrations exist yet, but the guide already gives a safe change checklist. New columns must be nullable or carry a DEFAULT, and generated SQL is reviewed with `dotnet ef migrations script`. Removing a column is split in two: the first deploy stops reading it by removing it from the EF configuration; the second deploy adds the migration that drops it. During a rolling deployment old instances still read the column, so dropping it first would break them.

- Dropping before the code change is exactly the downtime the checklist avoids.
- The order is stop reading first, then drop, not the reverse.
- Making it nullable is advice for adding columns, not removing them.

excerpts.quote: This two-step process prevents downtime from rolling deployment

items.title: The upskill tree: validation, persistence and a critique
items.body:
The newer questions come from `docs/upskill/`, a longer guide to the same codebase, mostly its architecture section.

`03-validation-auth-and-permissions.md` lays out the validation layers, how a request is authenticated, where authorization lives and how the tenant is resolved. `02-data-model-and-persistence.md` maps the tables and EF Core mappings, then covers context lifetime, change tracking, migrations, query shape and transaction boundaries. `06-architecture-critique.md` lists the strongest design choices and a prioritized set of risks, each labelled Confirmed, Hypothesis or Investigate, with suggested fixes. One flashcard also uses the integration-test flow from `01-codebase-cartography/05-key-flows.md`.

When a document proposes a fix, check the code it names: a suggested fix is a proposal, not something the repository already does.

excerpts.quote: Confirmed = inspected directly. Hypothesis = inferred from patterns. Investigate = needs verification.

readMore.why: The map of the whole upskill tree.

items.title: Why a token-less "anonymous" booking fails with 500
items.body:
The key is right. Without a JWT there is no `tenant_id` claim, so `CurrentTenantService.TenantId` is null. Line 21 does `currentTenant.TenantId!.Value`; the `!` only silences the compiler, and `.Value` on a null `Guid?` throws `InvalidOperationException`. The exception middleware turns that into a 500.

- `Items["TenantId"]` is set but never read.
- `[AllowAnonymous]` only skips the authorization check; it creates no tenant.
- Validation passes for a valid command, so the request reaches the handler and throws there.

excerpts.quote: var tenantId = TenantId.From(currentTenant.TenantId!.Value);
For an invitee with no token, `TenantId` is `null`

items.title: A class-level [Authorize] that blocks the public page
items.body:
EventTypesController carries [Authorize] at class level, and its GET by id has no [AllowAnonymous]. The public booking page, BookPage.tsx, calls that endpoint to load the event type, so an unauthenticated visitor gets a 401 and the public booking flow is broken. The critique suggests adding [AllowAnonymous] to GetById or creating a separate public endpoint that resolves user and event slugs.

- Hosts are authenticated, so they are not the ones refused.
- The problem is too much protection for visitors, not too little; the cross-tenant read issue is RISK-001.
- The booking POST lives on a different controller, so this class-level attribute does not reach it.

excerpts.quote: It will fail with 401 for unauthenticated visitors. The public booking flow is broken.

items.title: Check-then-insert with no constraint can double-book
items.body:
The key is right. The handler first asks for conflicting bookings (line 33), then adds and saves (lines 43-44). Two requests can both see "no conflict" and both insert. `BookingConfiguration` has an index on `(HostId, StartTime)`, but it is not unique, and there is no exclusion constraint on time ranges.

- The conflict query is a separate read, not part of a shared transaction with a lock.
- The index exists only for speed; it lacks `IsUnique()`.
- `BookingCreatedEvent` is published after save; nothing cancels bookings.

excerpts.quote: builder.HasIndex(b => new { b.HostId, b.StartTime });
The conflict query (line 33) and the insert (lines 43-44) share no transaction or constraint

items.title: Domain events go out only after a successful save
items.body:
The key is right. `SaveChangesAsync` collects the domain events and clears them from the entities, then awaits `base.SaveChangesAsync(ct)`, and only after that loops over `publisher.Publish`. If the base save throws, the method exits before the loop, so no event is published.

- Publishing comes after the save, so handlers cannot veto the write.
- There is no retry job; events lost with a failed save are simply gone.
- MediatR `Publish` is not part of the database transaction.

excerpts.quote: var result = await base.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
await publisher.Publish(domainEvent, ct);

items.title: The repo validates tokens but never issues them
items.body:
The API's JwtBearerHandler validates signature, issuer, audience and expiry, and handlers read the sub, tenant_id and tenant_slug claims. But nothing in the repository creates those tokens for real users: there is no login endpoint and no token generation. An external identity provider such as Auth0 or Keycloak has to issue them. The only token minting in the codebase is JwtTokenFactory in the integration tests, which signs test tokens with the same key as appsettings.json.

- There is no login endpoint at all.
- The tenant middleware stores an id in HttpContext.Items; it issues nothing.
- No seeded user or controller hands out tokens.

excerpts.quote: There's no login endpoint, no token generation.

items.title: What the old code did with a mismatched host
items.body:
The key is right. Before the fix, the only check was `eventType is null`. With E found, the handler used E's duration, searched H's bookings, and built a booking that joined E (owned by J) to H's calendar.

- No 403 existed: nothing compared the owner with the host.
- The foreign keys were satisfied, because both E and H exist; that is the guide's point.
- Nothing switched to J; the command's host was used as given.

excerpts.quote: searched H's bookings and constructed a booking connecting E to H.
if (eventType is null)

items.title: Core idea: an id sent by the caller is a claim, not proof
items.body:
A public booking request contains ids chosen by the caller: which event type, which host. Each id may name a real row, and still the combination can be wrong, for example an event that belongs to a different host.

A foreign key in the database only proves that a row exists. It does not prove that two rows belong together. So the handler must load the stored event and compare its own owner and tenant with what the request says. Read `02-CONCEPTS.md`, then find the comparison in both handlers and notice what work happens before it and what happens after it.

excerpts.quote: A foreign key can prove that a referenced row exists. It does not necessarily prove that two referenced rows belong together.
Caller-provided IDs are assertions to check, not authority.

items.title: Start here: two public endpoints and one ownership rule
items.body:
NetCalendy is a Calendly-style booking app: ASP.NET Core with MediatR handlers, EF Core on Postgres, and a React front end. Anyone may book a host's published event type, so two endpoints are public: create a booking, and list available slots.

The `astraupskill/` course is about one rule on those two paths. Read it in this order:

1. `01-CODEBASE-MAP.md`: the controller, the handler, and where the tenant really comes from.
2. `02-CONCEPTS.md`: why a request is a relationship between tenant, host and event.
3. `03-WORKED-CHANGE.md`: the one-line guard and where it sits.
4. `07-TRACE-LAB.md`: a table of inputs and results to fill in.
5. `06-SOLUTIONS-AND-REVIEW.md`: the review findings A to D that the change did not fix.

Keep `CreateBookingHandler.cs` open; it is 50 lines and most questions point into it.

excerpts.quote: accepts CreateBookingCommand on POST api/bookings with `[AllowAnonymous]`

readMore.why: The whole booking command handler, line by line.
The availability query handler with the same guard.

items.title: No default schedule means an empty, successful list
items.body:
The key is right. After the scope and active checks, the query handler calls `GetDefaultByUserAsync`. Line 31: `if (schedule is null) return Result.Success<...>([]);`. The bookings read on line 40 is never reached.

- NotFound is only for a missing or out-of-scope event.
- `Schedule.InvalidTimezone` needs a schedule whose timezone fails to parse.
- Slots come from a schedule; with none, there is nothing to offer.

excerpts.quote: if (schedule is null) return Result.Success<IReadOnlyList<AvailableSlotDto>>([]);
A matching event with no schedule returns an empty successful list (line 31).

items.title: A substring rule maps the conflict to 400
items.body:
The key is right. The handler fails with code `Booking.TimeConflict`. `ToActionResult` returns 409 only if the code contains `.Conflict`, `Taken` or `AlreadyCancelled`. `Booking.TimeConflict` contains `.TimeConflict`, so `.Conflict` (with the dot) is not a substring, and the switch falls to `_ => 400`.

- The controller's `ProducesResponseType(409)` is documentation; it does not change the mapping.
- 404 needs a code ending in `.NotFound`.
- No arm returns 422.

excerpts.quote: _ when error.Code.Contains(".Conflict") || error.Code.Contains("Taken")
_ when error.Code.Contains("Forbidden") => 403, _ => 400,

items.title: The controller rejects ranges over 60 days
items.body:
The key is right. `GetAvailableSlots` in `SchedulesController` checks `endDate < startDate` and then whether the span in days is greater than 60. For 61 days it returns `BadRequest("Date range cannot exceed 60 days.")` before `mediator.Send`.

- The handler never sees the request, so it cannot trim anything.
- Over-long ranges are refused, not only reversed ones.
- This check is in the controller, not in a MediatR `ValidationBehavior`.

excerpts.quote: return BadRequest("Date range cannot exceed 60 days.");
reject reversed ranges and ranges over sixty days before the mediator is called.

items.title: One answer for missing and mismatched
items.body:
The key is right. If a wrong host got a different error from a missing event, a caller could learn that an event id is real even though it belongs to someone else. Returning `Error.NotFound("EventType", ...)` for both cases hides that.

- `FindAsync` loads by primary key and does not look at the owner at all.
- There is no query filter on EventType; the only `HasQueryFilter` is on users.
- `ResultExtensions` maps several code families (404, 409, 403, 400), not only NotFound.

excerpts.quote: Returning the same not-found result for missing and mismatched resources avoids introducing a separate response
eventType.OwnerId != hostId

items.title: Resource-level authorization lives inside handlers
items.body:
NetCalendy has two authorization levels. Coarse-grained: [Authorize] on controller classes and [AllowAnonymous] on specific actions. Fine-grained policies do not exist: there is no IAuthorizationHandler and no policy. Questions like "may this user modify this event type?" are answered inline, as UpdateEventTypeHandler does by comparing the event type's OwnerId with the current user. The guide calls this correct behavior, but scattered rather than centralized.

- No policies are registered in Program.cs.
- Treating FluentValidation as the authorization layer is listed as a junior mistake.
- [Authorize] only requires an authenticated user; it carries no ownership logic.

excerpts.quote: This is correct behavior, but it's scattered across handlers rather than being in a centralized authorization policy.

items.title: One SaveChanges per handler is the transaction
items.body:
Each writing handler calls `uow.SaveChangesAsync()` once, at the end. EF Core wraps that save in an implicit transaction, so creating a User and a Schedule in one handler either both succeed or both fail. Call it twice and that guarantee splits in two: the first save commits permanently even if the second one fails, leaving half the work stored. The guide notes the repo has no such handler today but calls it a code review red flag.

- The second save does not re-insert rows the first already saved.
- EF allows several saves on one context; the problem is atomicity, not an error.
- No locking or deadlock is involved.

excerpts.quote: the first save commits permanently even if the second fails.
